definition: In computer science, constrained clustering is a class of semi-supervised learning algorithms.
details: Typically, constrained clustering incorporates either a set of must-link constraints, cannot-link constraints, or both, with a data clustering algorithm. A cluster in which the members conform to all must-link and cannot-link constraints is called a chunklet.

explainer.lead: Constrained clustering groups data while following extra instructions about which items must stay together and which must stay apart. It is useful when ordinary similarity measures are not enough to capture what a good grouping should look like.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting a box of toys into piles, but some toys are tied together and must go in the same pile, while two other toys are not allowed to share a pile. Constrained clustering does this with data: it makes groups while obeying those special instructions.
tiers.practitioner: Apply it by adding must-link and cannot-link pairs to a clustering algorithm, then checking both cluster quality and constraint violations. Constraint handling matters because violating a required pair is different from merely producing an imperfect similarity-based grouping; contradictory constraints can also leave no valid clustering.
tiers.paperLevel: Given data X, must-link pairs M, and cannot-link pairs C, constrained clustering seeks a partition in which every (x, y) in M has cluster(x) = cluster(y) and every (x, y) in C has cluster(x) != cluster(y). It is a class of semi-supervised learning algorithms, and a chunklet is a cluster whose members conform to all must-link and cannot-link constraints.

explainer.example: For six records A through F, require A and B to be together and C and D to be apart. One valid result is {A, B, E}, {C, F}, and {D}: A remains with B, C is separated from D, and each resulting cluster is a chunklet.
explainer.goal: Produce clusters that group similar data while satisfying specified must-link and cannot-link constraints.
inputs: Must-link pairs that must share a cluster
Cannot-link pairs that must occupy different clusters
outputs: A partition of the data into clusters
Chunklets whose members satisfy all applicable constraints
steps: Collect the data and the must-link and cannot-link pairs.
Supply the data and constraints to a clustering algorithm.
Form clusters while keeping must-linked items together and cannot-linked items apart.
Return the resulting partition and check that every constraint is satisfied.
tradeoffs: Constraints add desired knowledge but reduce the set of possible clusterings.
A similarity-based grouping may need to change to obey the constraints.
Contradictory constraints can make a valid clustering impossible.
